meta.theme: the requirement that a civil disobedient accept his punishment defended neither by sincerity nor by fidelity to law but by what submission does to the act, since remaining and taking the consequence is what keeps the claim addressed to the community that is being asked to think again, which makes the requirement constitutive rather than evidential and suspends it wherever the penalty is itself the injustice complained of

meta.reviewer_notes: The hard move is that submission is treated as constitutive rather than evidential, which most readers have no slot for, so several distractors offer it as a test, a proof or a payment. The final paragraph applies the definition to three cases, states a limit and then grants one of the rejected defences a real point, and the purpose question is decided by whether a reader kept the limit inside the purpose.
meta.tone: austere, analytic, conceding late and narrowly

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that the departing protester has committed an ordinary offence after all, which quietly deletes the publicity the first paragraph uses to separate him from the ordinary offender; what he loses by leaving is the address, and the passage says so by calling it a withdrawal of his own appeal. Q2's rival is the option that the requirement is a test which an act may fail, since failing it does remove the act from the category; the passage refuses the strength of the rest of that option by keeping the departing protester a protester, describing him as speaking from the aeroplane rather than as having stopped protesting. Q3's rival is the true option that a sincere man may still be wrong, which reads like the sort of thing a passage sets up to deny, and which is in fact the author's own reason for dismissing the sincerity defence. Q4's rival is the option about defending civil disobedience against a charge, which describes a purpose the passage never takes up, since the two arguments it demolishes are defences of the requirement rather than attacks on the practice.

paragraphs.text: Begin with the term, because the quarrel is mostly conducted without one. Civil disobedience is a breach of law that is public, announced rather than concealed, limited in its means, and addressed to the judgement of the community whose law it breaks. Each element does work. The publicity separates the disobedient from the ordinary offender, who hopes above all not to be noticed. The limitation on means separates him from the insurgent, who has no objection to being noticed and every objection to being judged. The address separates him from both, because it commits him to what neither accepts: that the community he defies is the body whose verdict he wants. The word conscience, which fills the literature, does very little of this work. A man may be as conscientious as he likes in a cellar.

A further requirement is usually attached: that the disobedient submit to the penalty. Two defences of it are in circulation and neither survives inspection. The first says that submission proves his sincerity. Sincerity is cheap to display and, more to the point, beside the question: a perfectly sincere man may be wrong about the law he is breaking, and an argument gains no force from the conviction of the person making it. The second says that submission demonstrates a fidelity to law as a whole, an obedience to the system offered in compensation for disobedience to a part of it. That produces the odd figure of a man defying and obeying at once, says nothing about which penalties are to be accepted, and reduces a serious requirement to a piece of etiquette.

What submission actually does is fix the addressee. A breach whose author remains where he is and takes what follows is a claim made inside the arrangement, to the people who maintain it and are being asked to think again. A breach whose author removes himself is a claim made from outside, and from outside the arrangement the act is not an appeal but an exit. On this account acceptance of the penalty proves nothing whatever about the man. It is constitutive rather than evidential: it is the thing that makes his act the kind of act the definition named, much as posting a letter is not evidence of an intention to communicate but the communicating itself.

Apply the definition and the cases sort themselves. The smuggler who breaks a law he believes unjust, and hides, has done nothing civil however sound his reasons: there is nobody he has addressed. The protester who breaks a law in the morning and is abroad by evening has withdrawn his own appeal, whatever he goes on saying from the aeroplane. The demonstrator who sits in the road and afterwards in the cell has done the whole of it, and the second sitting is not a payment for the first but its completion. One thing should be granted to the second rejected defence: a man who stays does display a relation to the law that a fugitive does not, though what he displays is a relation to the law rather than anything about his convictions, and a display may be dispensed with when nobody doubts it. The requirement holds only where the punishment can be separated from the complaint; where the penalty is itself the injustice objected to, submitting is not the price of being heard but a surrender of the point at issue, and nothing here demands it.

questions.target_mistake: treating the departing protester as having lost the publicity of his breach, when what he loses is the address, which is a different element of the definition
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the answer will name the element of the definition that leaving destroys, which is the address rather than the publicity or the sincerity.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that, on the author's account, a person who breaks a law in protest and then leaves the country has

options.A: shown that his objection to the law was never a conscientious one
options.B: changed the addressee of his act, so that what he did is no longer the appeal the definition named
options.C: forfeited whatever protection the law would otherwise have given him
options.D: committed an ordinary offence after all, since the publicity of the breach now counts for nothing

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph draws the line for exactly this case. A breach whose author remains is a claim made inside the arrangement to the people who maintain it; a breach whose author removes himself is a claim made from outside, and from outside the act is an exit rather than an appeal. The fourth paragraph then applies it, saying such a protester has withdrawn his own appeal.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option states that application in the definition's own vocabulary. Leaving does not undo the breach, and it does not undo the publicity: the act was announced and is still announced. What it undoes is the commitment to the community's verdict, which the first paragraph named as the element separating the disobedient from everybody else. That is one honest step from two sentences the author has already joined.
explanation.question_type_note: Where a passage defines a term by elements, an inference about a case is usually a question about which element the case fails. Name the element before reading the options.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author separates a category from its neighbours by three or four features, keep them apart in your notes. Distractors in such passages are built by removing the wrong feature.

distractors.why_wrong: The account is explicitly silent about the man. The third paragraph says acceptance of the penalty proves nothing whatever about him, and the second has already dismissed sincerity as cheap to display and beside the question, so nothing here licenses a verdict on his conscience.
distractors.seductive_element: Conscience is the vocabulary everybody brings to this subject, and a reader who has not noticed the first paragraph pushing it aside will reach for it when asked what leaving reveals.

distractors.why_wrong: Protections and their forfeiture are nowhere in the passage. The argument concerns what an act is, not what its author is then entitled to, and no consequence of any kind is attached to flight beyond the loss of the address.
distractors.seductive_element: Flight from justice carries a heavy legal association, and readers supply the penalty that usually attends it.

distractors.why_wrong: The first clause is a possible conclusion and the second clause names the wrong loss. Publicity is unaffected by leaving, and it is publicity that the first paragraph uses to separate the disobedient from the ordinary offender, who hopes above all not to be noticed.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the man really has fallen out of the category, and the ordinary offender is the nearest thing the passage offers to put him in.

questions.target_mistake: reading the requirement as a test applied to acts from outside the definition, rather than as the thing that makes one element of the definition true
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before the options: submission is not evidence for the definition and not an addition to it, but the way one of its elements gets satisfied.
questions.stem: The relation between the requirement of submission and the definition offered in the first paragraph is best described as follows:

options.A: the requirement is a separate moral demand, owed to the law rather than to the community
options.B: the definition was derived from the requirement, which the tradition had fixed first
options.C: the requirement is a further test, so that an act which fails it, though still unlawful, ceases to be a protest of any kind
options.D: the requirement is what makes one element of the definition true of a particular act

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph says it in a single sentence and then explains it with an example. Acceptance of the penalty is constitutive rather than evidential, and posting a letter is not evidence of an intention to communicate but the communicating itself. The element it constitutes is the address, which the first paragraph had already made part of the definition.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps that relation. The definition requires the act to be addressed to the community's judgement, and staying is how an act comes to be so addressed; the requirement therefore sits inside the definition rather than beside it. This is also why the author can say the second sitting is not a payment for the first but its completion, a sentence no evidential account could produce.
explanation.question_type_note: A relationship question asks what one thing is to another: an example, a cause, a contrast, a condition or a part. The answer is a structural word, not a summary of either item.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author writes that something is constitutive rather than evidential, stop and check what it constitutes. The distinction reorganises everything that follows, and options that ignore it will all sound plausible.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second rejected defence in different clothes, which the passage refuses for producing a man defying and obeying at once. It also puts the requirement outside the definition, whereas the third paragraph places it inside by making it the thing the definition's own element consists in.
distractors.seductive_element: A duty owed to law as a system is the most familiar account of this requirement in the literature, and the passage discusses it at length before setting it aside.

distractors.why_wrong: The order of the passage is the reverse and so is the argument. The definition is set out first and defended element by element, and the requirement is then shown to follow from it; no history of the tradition is given anywhere.
distractors.seductive_element: The requirement is introduced as something usually attached by others, which sounds like an inheritance the author is working backwards from.

distractors.why_wrong: Failing the requirement removes an act from this category and not from every category. The protester who leaves is still described as protesting, going on saying things from the aeroplane, and what he has lost is the address rather than the character of protest altogether.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because failing the requirement really does put an act outside the definition, and the extra step from that to ceasing to be a protest is made in one word.

questions.target_mistake: keeping the sincerity defence as part of the author's account because it is the reason most often given for the requirement outside the passage
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true, according to the passage?

options.A: A disobedient who accepts his punishment thereby shows that his objection was sincerely held.
options.B: A man may be entirely sincere in his objection and still be wrong about the law he is breaking.
options.C: An act carried out in secret falls outside the definition, however strong the conviction that produced it.
options.D: The requirement of submission lapses where the penalty is itself the injustice objected to.

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph names the sincerity defence and knocks it down twice over, calling sincerity cheap to display and then beside the question. The third paragraph finishes it off with a flat sentence: acceptance of the penalty proves nothing whatever about the man.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the sincerity defence restated as though the passage held it. Everything in the argument runs the other way: the requirement is said to do something to the act rather than to reveal anything about its author, which is why the third paragraph can say in so many words that acceptance of the penalty proves nothing whatever about the man, and why the concession at the close is careful to call the display a relation to the law rather than a sign of conviction.
explanation.question_type_note: A NOT-true question is a verification exercise. Check each option against the text in turn; the false one usually reverses a direction or restores a claim the passage has removed.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage rejects a familiar justification, expect to meet that justification again among the options, stated calmly and without attribution. The question is whether you noticed the rejection, not whether the sentence sounds sensible.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second paragraph's own reason for dismissing the sincerity defence, reordered: a perfectly sincere man may be wrong about the law he is breaking, and an argument gains no force from the conviction of the person making it.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it sounds like the sort of sceptical remark a passage introduces in order to reject it, and a reader matching words rather than claims will not find it verbatim.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph says precisely this of the smuggler, who has done nothing civil however sound his reasons, because there is nobody he has addressed. The strength of the phrase about conviction matches the passage's own dismissal of conscience in a cellar.
distractors.seductive_element: The sweeping clause invites the suspicion that the passage must have hedged somewhere, and readers hunt for a qualification that was never made.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the limit stated in the fourth paragraph, where the requirement is said to hold only if the punishment can be separated from the complaint, and where submitting to a penalty that is itself the injustice is called a surrender of the point at issue.
distractors.seductive_element: A reader who has absorbed how firmly the requirement is defended will treat any exception to it as an invention of the option writer.

questions.target_mistake: taking the purpose to be a defence of civil disobedience itself, when what is being argued about throughout is the ground of one requirement attached to it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to name a verb and an object: throw out two justifications of a requirement, supply a third from the definition, and mark where it ceases to bind.
questions.stem: The author's purpose in the passage is chiefly

options.A: to defend civil disobedience against the charge that it is lawbreaking with a good conscience, and to say when the defence fails
options.B: to trace how the requirement that a disobedient accept punishment entered political thought, and why it survived
options.C: to replace two bad reasons for a familiar requirement with a reason drawn from the definition, and to say where it stops
options.D: to argue that a protester ought to submit to punishment whenever the law he breaks is a just one

explanation.expert_notice: The shape of the passage announces the purpose. A definition is fixed, two defences of the attached requirement are demolished in one paragraph, a third ground is supplied in the next, and the last paragraph applies it to three cases and then states the condition under which the requirement lapses.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries all three movements. The two bad reasons are sincerity and fidelity; the good reason is that submission fixes the addressee and so satisfies an element already in the definition; the stopping point is the case where the penalty is itself the injustice. A purpose that drops the last of these leaves a paragraph of the passage with nothing to do, and the author has written it as a limit rather than as an aside.
explanation.question_type_note: Purpose is a verb with an object, and in a passage that rejects and replaces, the replacement plus its limits is the object. Never the material being rejected.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask which paragraph a candidate purpose would let you delete. The purpose that leaves every paragraph earning its place is the one the author was working to.

distractors.why_wrong: The conscience material is real and its job in the passage is a different one. The first paragraph pushes conscience aside in order to clear room for the definition, not in order to answer anybody hostile to disobedience, and the two arguments demolished afterwards are defences of the requirement offered by its friends.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does push conscience aside briskly, which reads like impatience with a slogan used against protesters rather than with one used in their favour.

distractors.why_wrong: There is no history in the passage, and nothing about the requirement's survival. It is introduced as something usually attached to the definition, and the whole argument concerns what would justify it rather than when or how it was first made.
distractors.seductive_element: The phrase about two defences being in circulation sounds like the opening of an intellectual history, and readers expect political theory to arrive with a lineage.

distractors.why_wrong: The condition is the wrong one and the passage never issues the advice. What the fourth paragraph makes decisive is whether the punishment can be separated from the complaint, not whether the law broken was just, and a disobedient who thought the law just would not be disobeying it.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does end by drawing a line, and a reader who has registered that a condition exists may fill it in with the most familiar criterion in the field.

vocabulary.meaning_here: one who takes up arms against the authority itself

vocabulary.passage_use: It is constitutive rather than evidential
vocabulary.meaning_here: part of what makes a thing what it is, rather than a sign of it

vocabulary.passage_use: reduces a serious requirement to a piece of etiquette
vocabulary.meaning_here: a rule of good form, carrying no weight of its own

vocabulary.passage_use: demonstrates a fidelity to law as a whole
vocabulary.meaning_here: faithfulness to a thing taken as a whole, shown in conduct

mentor.challenge: A familiar rule is given a new ground, and the new ground is of a kind most readers have no slot for. Watch the sentence that calls the rule constitutive rather than evidential, because two of the four questions are settled by whether you took it seriously.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The rule that a civil disobedient must take his punishment is usually justified as proof of sincerity or as a display of loyalty to law, and neither justification works, whereas staying and taking the consequence is what keeps the act addressed to the community whose verdict is being asked for, which makes the rule part of what the act is rather than evidence about the man, and which suspends it exactly where the penalty is itself the thing complained of.
mentor.main_idea: Civil disobedience is defined by four things, the important one being that the act is addressed to the judgement of the community whose law it breaks. The usual defences of the further rule that the disobedient must accept punishment both fail: sincerity is irrelevant to an argument, and loyalty to the system makes the rule mere good manners. The real answer is that staying is what makes the act an appeal to those people rather than an exit from their arrangement. So the rule is part of the act, not a proof about its author, and it lapses where the punishment is itself the injustice.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Start with what the words mean, because most arguments about this skip that step. Civil disobedience is breaking a law in a way that is public, announced beforehand, limited in what it will do, and aimed at the judgement of the very community whose law is being broken.

Every part of that is doing a job. Being public is what separates this person from an ordinary criminal, who above all does not want to be seen. Limiting the means is what separates him from an armed rebel, who does not mind being seen but will not accept anybody's verdict. And aiming the act at the community is what separates him from both, because it means he is treating the people he is defying as the people whose judgement he wants. Notice that the word conscience does almost none of this work. You can be as sincere as you like in a cellar, and nobody would call that civil disobedience.

Then there is the extra rule everyone attaches: that the person must accept his punishment. Two reasons are usually given, and the author throws out both. The first is that accepting punishment proves he means it. But proving you mean it is easy, and it is also not the point: a completely sincere person can still be wrong about the law, and an argument does not get stronger because the person making it feels strongly. The second reason is that accepting punishment shows loyalty to the legal system as a whole, even while breaking one part of it. That gives you the strange picture of a man obeying and disobeying at the same moment, tells you nothing about which punishments he has to accept, and turns a serious rule into good manners.

Here is the author's answer. What accepting the punishment really does is decide who the act is speaking to. If you stay and take what comes, you are making a claim inside the arrangement, to the people who run it, asking them to think again. If you run, you are making a claim from outside, and from outside it is not an appeal at all; it is a departure. So accepting the punishment proves nothing about you. It is what makes the act the kind of act the definition described, in the same way that posting a letter is not proof that you meant to communicate. It is the communicating.

Now apply it. The smuggler who breaks a law he thinks unjust and hides has done nothing civil, however good his reasons, because there is nobody he has spoken to. The protester who breaks a law in the morning and is on a plane by evening has cancelled his own appeal, whatever he says afterwards. The demonstrator who sits in the road and then sits in the cell has done the whole thing, and the cell is not a payment for the road; it is the finish of it.

And there is a limit. The rule only works when the punishment can be separated from the complaint. If the punishment is itself the injustice you are objecting to, then submitting is not the price of being heard. It is giving away the very thing you came to argue about, and nothing in this account asks you to.

Finally he gives the loyalty answer one thing back. Someone who stays really does show a relationship to the law that a runaway does not, and that is a real difference. But showing something is not what makes the rule binding, because a show can be skipped when nobody doubts you, and this rule cannot be skipped.
mentor.why_difficult: The central move, that a requirement can be part of an act rather than evidence about its author, is unfamiliar, and readers who miss it convert the rule back into a test or a proof at the first opportunity, which is what three of the distractors are built from. The second difficulty is that the definition has four elements and the cases fail different ones, so an answer requires knowing which element leaving destroys rather than merely that something has been destroyed. The third is the last paragraph, which applies, limits and concedes in quick succession, with the concession arriving after most readers have decided the argument is over.
mentor.author_intention: To get a familiar requirement off the two grounds that cannot hold it and onto one that can, so that the reader stops treating the acceptance of punishment as a gesture of good faith and starts treating it as the part of the act that decides whom the act is speaking to.

paragraph_journey.note: Public, announced, limited, and addressed to the community. Each element keeps the disobedient apart from the criminal and the rebel. Conscience does very little.
Sincerity is cheap and beside the point. Loyalty to the system produces a man obeying and disobeying at once, and turns the rule into etiquette.
Staying decides who the act is addressed to. It proves nothing about the man; it is what makes the act the thing the definition named.
The smuggler, the departing protester, the demonstrator in the cell. The loyalty account is granted one real point and no more. And the rule lapses where the penalty is itself the injustice.

mentor.tone_progression: It begins impatient with a debate conducted without definitions, turns coolly destructive through the two defences, becomes precise and almost technical at the sentence that names the requirement constitutive, and ends measured, working through cases and then handing a rejected argument exactly one thing.
key_transitions: 'What submission actually does is fix the addressee.' (opening of paragraph 3): the requirement is taken off evidence and put onto structure.
'It is constitutive rather than evidential' (paragraph 3): the distinction on which the whole replacement rests.
'The requirement holds only where the punishment can be separated from the complaint' (paragraph 4): the rule is given its boundary.
mentor.misunderstanding: The usual wrong model is that the passage is defending civil disobedience against people who dislike it. It is not: both positions it destroys are held by the practice's friends, and the argument throughout is about what could justify one rule. The second wrong model keeps the sincerity account alive in the background, so that submission ends up meaning that the protester really means it, which the passage denies in a sentence of its own by saying acceptance proves nothing whatever about the man.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers a rejected defence restated as the passage's view, the wrong element of the definition as the thing flight destroys, the requirement as a test rather than as a constituent, an ordinary criticism of protest as the purpose, and a familiar criterion slotted into a limit the passage defined differently. Sorting every option by which paragraph it belongs to answers all four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage fixes a definition by elements and then argues about a rule attached to it, do not ask whether the rule is right; ask which element it serves, because that is what every question will turn on. The companion habit is to take seriously any sentence that distinguishes being evidence for something from being part of it: authors who draw that distinction have changed the kind of claim under discussion, and every option written in the old kind will feel familiar and be wrong.
mentor.real_world: The same structure appears wherever a formality turns out to be constitutive rather than symbolic: a signature that does not prove agreement but makes the agreement, a resignation that is not evidence of leaving but the leaving, a guilty plea that does not show remorse but ends the trial. Arguments about whether such acts are sincere usually miss what the act is doing.
mentor.takeaway: Staying is not the proof that you were appealing to them; staying is the appeal.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the objections you make are addressed to the people who could answer them, and which are made on your way out of the door?

eli10.big_idea: Staying to take the punishment is part of civil disobedience itself: it keeps the protest speaking to the community; it proves nothing about sincerity.
eli10.story: Civil disobedience means breaking a law openly, by limited means, to ask your community to think again. A thief hides; this protester announces. A rebel wants to win; this protester wants to be judged. Strong feelings are not enough. You can feel strongly in a cellar. People also say the protester must accept the punishment. The writer rejects the two usual reasons. The first says it proves he is sincere. Yet sincere people can be wrong; sincerity adds nothing to an argument. The second says it shows respect for the law. That turns a serious rule into good manners. The real reason: staying keeps the protest speaking to the community. Running away turns an appeal into an exit. It is like posting a letter. Posting is not proof you wanted to talk. It is the talking. One limit: if the punishment itself is the injustice, nobody need accept it.
paragraphs: Defines civil disobedience: open, limited lawbreaking aimed at the community's judgement, not just strong feeling.
Rejects the two usual reasons for accepting punishment: proving sincerity, and showing loyalty to the law.
Gives the real reason: staying keeps the protest an appeal to the community, not an exit.
Sorts cases with it, grants one small point, and excuses anyone whose punishment is itself the injustice.
eli10.author_view: The writer is precise and a little impatient with loose talk, firmly dismissing weak reasons and naming clear limits.
